source.title: (Mis)Understanding Benign Overfitting in Equity Return Prediction
source.authors: Hui Guo; Jia-Wei Huang; Run-Ze Li; Yan Yu

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures out-of-sample risk across feature counts in a ridgeless random Fourier feature regression, rather than reproducing the original deep-network method.
record.gate_note: The relevant empirical result is Figure 1's risk-versus-parameter-to-observation-ratio sweep, plus the paper's own theoretical result for the optimal ridge penalty under the zero-slope null. Results on portfolio Sharpe ratios, momentum strategies, and forecasts are not risk-versus-size, epoch, or sample-size results for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study applies ridgeless random Fourier feature regression to equity-return prediction. It reports test risk against P/T for three training windows (Figure 1), showing a spike at γ=1 and a second descent. It also proves and shows that heavy or optimal ridge removes the peak under a zero-slope null. These bear on V4 and V6 in a new, finance setting. It is not a deep-network replication.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Ridgeless RFF shows genuine double descent, but that does not imply bigger models forecast better. Under zero true slopes the optimal ridge penalty is infinite, collapsing the model to the historical average. Empirically, ridgeless, CV-tuned and heavily regularized RFF models track that average and add negligible market-timing ability. KMZ's apparent gains come from the omitted intercept and non-centered features.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps random Fourier feature counts in ridge regression for equity-return prediction, rather than testing deep networks as in the original model-size experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The Figure 1 risk curves are reported for training windows T = 12, 60, and 120 months; the risk pattern is for the ridgeless estimator, while the fixed z = 10⁹ comparator has lower risk.

fits_no_version.finding: Double descent appears even with zero true signal. The peak is pure variance, σ²/(γ−1), and the second descent only returns risk to the noise floor (the historical-average forecast). It never beats that forecast: ridgeless OOS R² is −0.01 to −0.02 at P=12,000.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Double descent can arise under a pure-noise target, where the second descent recovers only the trivial predictor's risk rather than improving on it.

record.problems: Figure 1 provides no exact risk values or uncertainty estimates in the text. Its curves are described as averaging 100 independent RFF generations, and the text says empirical curves continue declining and plateau beyond the displayed γ = 5. The empirical test is limited to this RFF ridge setting.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results directly measure test risk across model size, epochs, or sample size; portfolio performance and momentum comparisons are therefore omitted.

untested.parts: Deep networks are not studied; the model is RFF ridge regression only.
No curve over training epochs is reported.
Risk is plotted against γ for three T values, but not against sample size at fixed P. Whether more data raises risk near interpolation is not examined.
Only one model class (RFF ridgeless) is tested. The subsumption of the classical U-curve is not tested; under the null the left side is variance-only, so there is no first descent to compare.
No single complexity measure is tested as predicting peak location across axes.

Label noise is not varied, multiple or triple peaks are not examined, and optimal penalty is not tuned per γ in a risk sweep. The variance-driven peak is argued from Hastie et al.'s decomposition, not measured.
EDF is defined and CV-selected EDF medians are reported, but risk is never plotted against EDF. Whether the second descent becomes U-shaped under EDF is not tested.

missing.what: Ridgeless RFF at P=12,000 (γ=1000 for T=12) gives OOS R² of −0.02, −0.01 and −0.01 relative to the historical average. This is the far-right end of the second descent and still slightly worse than the benchmark. Similar small negatives appear for T=60 and 120.
CV-tuned ridge chooses z=10^9 in 47.68%, 44.26% and 41.79% of months (T=12, 60, 120). Median EDF is 2.49, 20.91 and 40.84, against nominal P=12,000. CV OOS R² is about −0.01 to 0.01.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche is T3 rather than T2: a new setting (finance, weak signal), not a different method on the original question. Figure 1 gives no numeric risk values. V4 support is limited to one model class, and the second descent there reaches only the noise floor.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses random Fourier feature ridge regression, not deep networks; it does not test the claimed deep-network model-size curve.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
The paper varies training-window lengths in its risk figure but does not test whether increasing sample size near interpolation raises test error.
The empirical curve is for ridgeless random Fourier feature regression only; it does not establish the pattern across model classes generally or test whether it subsumes the classical U-shaped curve.
Although effective degrees of freedom is discussed as a complexity measure, the study does not test whether one measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample size.

The study derives the optimal-regularization result under a zero-slope null, but does not vary label noise, test multiple or triple peaks, or empirically sweep an optimally tuned penalty across model sizes.
The study does not plot or measure the second descent against effective parameter count to determine whether it becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: heavily regularized ridge RFF estimator (z = 10⁹)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep feature count P and plot out-of-sample test risk against γ = P/T
rows.measure: Out-of-sample test risk (mean squared error) versus γ
rows.baseline: corresponding ridgeless estimator; exact risk not stated
rows.note: The text says this heavily regularized benchmark has strictly lower risk across γ and virtually overlays its historical-average forecast. This is a fixed penalty, not the optimally tuned penalty in V6.
rows.check: State should be observed, not cannot_determine. The z=10^9 curve has strictly lower risk across all γ and overlays the historical average, so there is no peak. Under the null, z*=∞ (Theorem 1), so z=10^9 approximates the optimal penalty. CV picks 10^9 in 47.68% of months. It remains a fixed penalty, not one tuned per γ.

rows.subject: ridge regression under the zero-slope null
rows.operation_detail: Derive the optimal ridge penalty and prediction error under the zero-slope null
rows.measure: Optimal penalty and asymptotic prediction error
rows.note: The authors state that the optimally regularized model bypasses the double-descent curve and collapses to the historical average under this null.
rows.check: This is an asymptotic theoretical result under β=0 with isotropic or bounded-spectrum features, not an empirical measurement. It builds on Hastie et al. (2022) Corollary 6.

relationships.condition: Ridgeless RFF regression on monthly equity returns, T = 12, 60, 120 months, averaged over 100 RFF draws
relationships.reason: Risk spikes at γ=1 and then declines as γ grows, plateauing beyond γ=5 (r1–r3, figure only). The descent reaches only the noise floor and never beats the historical average.
relationships.display_finding: Risk spiked at γ = 1, declined as γ increased, and plateaued beyond γ = 5 at the noise floor without outperforming the historical average.

relationships.condition: Zero-slope null; heavily or optimally regularized ridge RFF
relationships.reason: Theory gives z*=∞ with PE→σ², bypassing the peak (r7). The z=10^9 curves show no peak and lie below ridgeless at all γ (r4–r6).
relationships.display_finding: The optimum z*=∞ gave prediction error approaching σ², while z=10^9 produced peak-free curves below ridgeless error at every γ.

relation.reason: Its feature-count sweeps directly test post-interpolation risk descent, and its ridge analysis tests removal of the peak under regularization.

tranche.reason: The study tests double descent in a new application setting, equity-return prediction, and reports its own RFF risk curves. Its baseline comparison qualifies forecasting benefits without contradicting V4's curve-shape claim.
